102zhmb09yv: There are five gas parameters. SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST is COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS if source is cold and WARM_ACCESS if it is warm. SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS is SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST + WARM_ACCESS, SETCODEFROM_CURRENT_ACCESS_GAS is WARM_ACCESS, SETCODEFROM_WRITE_GAS is ACCOUNT_WRITE, and SETCODEFROM_STATE_GAS is 0. Each execution attempt first charges SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS. It is the sum of loading the source account leaf (SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST) and verifying the source code (WARM_ACCESS, a fixed cost covering the code storage access needed to inspect the bytecode). Once this charge is made, source is added to EIP-2929's accessed_addresses regardless of validity. Verification reads only source's own code and does not follow EIP-7702 delegation, so the delegation target is not accessed, charged, or warmed. If source is valid, SETCODEFROM_CURRENT_ACCESS_GAS is charged, the two code hashes are compared, and if they differ SETCODEFROM_WRITE_GAS is charged and the update is made. The write cost follows ACCOUNT_WRITE from EIP-8038. Based on the current EIP-8038 values (ACCOUNT_WRITE 9000, COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS 3000, WARM_ACCESS 100), an invalid source costs 3100 when cold and 200 when warm, a valid source with the same hash costs 3200 and 300, and an actual update costs 12200 and 9300. Because there is no code storage work, the cost is independent of the source code size, and it is the same when executed inside initcode. The state gas for adding an account leaf at creation itself may be incurred separately.

10rgzh6zk5d: Chunks have no individual signatures. Authenticity comes entirely from the bid signature through payload_chunks_root. The root carried in a chunk is not authenticated by itself, but a chunk is accepted only if a bid that passed signature verification committed to that root. A chunk that points to an unknown root is not forwarded, so unsigned chunk spam is filtered out at the first hop. slot and beacon_block_root are included in neither the bid signature nor the inclusion proof, so they are restricted to lookup use only. A chunk resent with a changed slot fails the (slot, payload_chunks_root) membership check, and a chunk with a changed beacon_block_root is rejected once the block containing the bid is known. Chunk bytes are bound to the proof, so a message that differs only in the hint fields cannot alter the reassembled envelope. For two different chunks at the same (payload_chunks_root, index) to both verify, a Merkle tree collision would be required, so per-index chunk equivocation is impossible. The upper bound on chunk.index is a key safeguard. is_valid_merkle_branch reads only the low CHUNK_INCLUSION_PROOF_DEPTH bits, so without the bound the same chunk could be spread again as index + k * TOTAL_EXECUTION_PAYLOAD_CHUNKS. Buffering before the block is also bounded. A node stores at most TOTAL_EXECUTION_PAYLOAD_CHUNKS chunks per payload_chunks_roots entry, and the size of that set is limited by bid gossip validation (the builder signature and the slot window). A chunk passing gossip validation does not make the reassembled envelope valid, and full envelope validation takes place after reassembly, as in EIP-7732.

10ypefci94v: Currently the SELFDESTRUCT instruction deletes the code and storage of a contract account entirely and sends the remaining ether to a specified address. This is an operation that changes account state significantly. Ethereum plans to hold state in a new data structure called a Verkle tree. In a Verkle tree, one account's data is stored scattered across multiple keys, and it is not visible from the outside which account those keys belong to. As a result, deleting an entire account becomes practically impossible. The source document explains that removing this instruction is a necessary condition for statelessness, where nodes do not need to hold the full state. On the other hand, there is no strong reason to need SELFDESTRUCT as it stands today, and apps that use it only to recover funds keep working after the change. So the proposal is to replace the instruction with a simple behavior that only sends ether, instead of removing it.

11c4irwj6v: Deploying the same code to many addresses is very common onchain, and smart account wallets are the prime example. To reduce deployment cost, ERC-1167 clones or upgradeable proxies are used. Clones are lightweight but their implementation address cannot be changed, while proxies can be changed but pay the cost of reading the implementation address from storage on every call. Both need EVM code that copies the received calldata into memory and performs a delegate call. According to a Geth team survey (EthCC[9] "Not all state is equal"), 97.1% of about 50 million deployed contracts are code that has already been deployed before, and 28.6% of unique bytecode is small code under 1 KiB. Clones and proxies likely make up a large share of that, so a way is needed to handle this role at the protocol level more compactly and cheaply.

11kytcdvmtf: Running a testnet for a long time causes problems to accumulate. Transaction history and state data keep growing, making it heavy to bring up a new node, and the faucet that hands out test coins runs out of funds. Even if the validator set grows bloated or a consensus problem arises, there is no way to roll back. This EIP standardizes periodically resetting the network to genesis. At each reset the validator set is emptied, funds return to the faucet, and the database stays small. Because each network's genesis is computed by a set rule, short-lived networks that come and go can be run repeatedly on a single test infrastructure. 11qhj9ybx8r: Today on Ethereum, the penalty a validator receives for missing an attestation (a vote on a block) does not depend on how other validators behaved. A validator that misses alone and one that misses together with 30% of the network pay exactly the same penalty each epoch. As a result there is almost no economic reason to diversify across nodes, regions, clients, internet providers and cloud vendors, because the only benefit is lowering the probability that all validators stop at once. Historical attestation data shows that validators under the same operator miss together far more often than chance, while solo stakers behave almost independently. Penalizing correlated failure can reduce the economies of scale of large, homogeneous staking operations without having to identify the operating entity. The protocol already prices correlated failure, but only when a third or more of the stake stops and the inactivity leak turns on. In the range below that, from 1% to 33%, correlated failure is effectively free. This EIP smoothly attaches a cost proportional to the size of the event in that range.

12spzoen52x: Following FIPS 204, the precompile computes ML-DSA.Verify(pubkey, message, signature) over the raw message. It also performs the matrix expansion Â = ExpandA(ρ) and the internal hash μ = H(BytesToBits(tr) ‖ M') itself, and returns success only when verification passes. Malformed encodings, such as coefficients out of range, a non-canonical hint h, or a ‖z‖ bound violation, MUST return failure rather than revert. This is so that callers can treat 'invalid signature' as a boolean. The output is always exactly 32 bytes. 0x00..01 is a valid signature, and 0x00..00 is an invalid or malformed signature, or an input shorter than PK_LEN + SIG_LEN. Because it does not revert except on gas exhaustion, the call success flag carries no signature information, and calling code must check the returned word with ISZERO along with the success flag. The fixed-length return is a deliberate difference from ECRECOVER and the EIP-7951 secp256r1 verification, which return an empty byte string on failure. A call to an address with no code also succeeds and returns an empty value, so with the empty-value approach 'invalid signature' and 'fork not activated or address not assigned on this chain' are byte-for-byte identical. This is the repeated complaint about P256VERIFY. In this proposal, a return length other than 32 means the precompile is absent, and 32 zero bytes means the signature failed. The cost is one word of memory and the accidental fail-closed behavior that Solidity gained when decoding an empty return value, and nothing more.

The burden is greater for zkEVMs, which verify EVM execution with zero-knowledge proofs, because each precompile needs a separate optimized non-EVM implementation. 13d7wetfkin: The new topic name is data_row_{subnet_id}, which is different from the deprecated blob_sidecar_{subnet_id}. Row subnets must use cell-level deltas (EIP-8136) without eager push, and the GroupID is the block root, as with column subnets. The function that assigns blobs to subnets, get_blob_row_subnet(blob_index, slot), is a per-slot pseudorandom permutation that applies compute_shuffled_index seeded with hash(b"ROW_SUBNET" + uint_to_bytes(uint64(slot))). If the blob count is at most ROW_SUBNET_COUNT, the blobs in a slot receive different subnets. If it is larger, blobs whose remainder after division by ROW_SUBNET_COUNT is the same share a subnet, so each subnet carries at most ceil(blob_count / ROW_SUBNET_COUNT) rows. Because the seed depends only on the slot, it can be computed without chain state. A node's designated row subnet is determined by get_row_subnet(node_id), which is the remainder after dividing bytes [8:16] of hash(uint_to_bytes(uint256(node_id))) by ROW_SUBNET_COUNT. Custody group derivation uses bytes [0:8] of the same hash, so the two assignments are independent of each other at no extra hashing cost. A row reconstructor must subscribe to its designated row subnet (MUST), and other nodes are recommended to subscribe when they support cell-level deltas (SHOULD). Subscribing carries no obligation to retain data.

13ezc7qt9oe: The gas cost of an operation that touches state is seen as the sum of up to three independent components. The first is Access, the cost of reading an account or storage slot from the database. COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS, COLD_STORAGE_ACCESS and WARM_ACCESS belong here, and they are renamed EIP-2929 parameters. This EIP raises only COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS and leaves the other two and the cold and warm determination rules unchanged. The second is Write, the cost of writing a leaf when a value changes. Storage slots pay STORAGE_WRITE, and the nonce, balance and code hash of an account pay ACCOUNT_WRITE, and both are constants newly created by this EIP. In the existing scheme, this share was dissolved inside composite constants such as GAS_STORAGE_UPDATE, CALL_VALUE and GAS_CREATE. STORAGE_WRITE is netted per transaction. The SSTORE that moves a slot away from its value at the start of the transaction pays it, and the SSTORE that later reverts it is refunded. ACCOUNT_WRITE is paid per operation. Making a value-bearing CALL to the same recipient twice pays it twice. The rule of paying only once per authority when processing EIP-7702 authorizations exists only in EIP-2780. The third is State creation, which is GAS_STORAGE_SET for a new slot and GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT for a new account. This EIP does not change these values, and EIP-8037 reprices them in the state gas dimension.

A content-hash-based message ID carries no context about which block a cell belongs to, so a node cannot request or prioritize missing cells. So one higher-level table can be built by merging the 4 tables (a fixed number) of the level directly below. 14kra0swddm: Consensus liveness: the builder for slot N+1 cannot build a canonical block before it receives the lists gossiped in slot N. Builders (including proposers who build blocks themselves) therefore need good connectivity to committee members, and there must be enough time between the view freeze (t=9s of slot N) and block propagation to collect the lists and update the payload. Equivocation: a P2P rule propagates at most two lists per member. If two different lists from the same member are seen, all of that member's lists are ignored. In the worst case, gossip subnet bandwidth can double. Payload construction: a naive approach that checks the lists' missing transactions against the post-state, appends a valid one to the end, and then restarts the check from the beginning can require n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... checks for n transactions, that is, O(n^2) checks. One example is when only the nth transaction is valid, and its execution sends balance to the sender of the (n-1)th transaction, making each one valid in turn. Instead, before building the payload, the builder can store the nonce and balance of every EOA involved in the list transactions and update them only when a nonce rises or a balance changes without a nonce change (for example, when an account abstraction transaction interacted with that EOA), which lets it judge validity in real time.

The more stake grows, the longer the queue gets. In practice, during the Kiln validator mass exit the queue exceeded 40 days. However, modern security hardware such as the iPhone Secure Enclave (Apple Secure Enclave), Android Keystore, and FIDO2/WebAuthn devices that log in with fingerprint or face recognition mostly create keys and sign with a different curve, secp256r1 (P-256). Verifying these signatures on Ethereum is currently prohibitively expensive or practically impossible. 16nwfkxtuz0: Every reconstruction duty arises only when the node holds at least 64 distinct verified cells of that row. Subscribing alone does not count as holding. Nodes that are not row reconstructors are also recommended to collect at least 64 cells for each row of their designated row subnet and announce this by bitmap (SHOULD). The row subnet pools the custody cells of its members, so the cells need not be in the node's own custody. Phase 1: a row reconstructor must recover the rows assigned to its designated row subnet that have enough cells (MUST) and update its bitmap. This is possible with its own column subscriptions alone, and a short random delay (recommended range TBD) avoids simultaneous execution across nodes. Phase 2: after collecting cells from getBlobs, columns and rows during a somewhat longer random delay (TBD), a supernode should recover all missing rows (SHOULD), and other row reconstructors may do so (MAY). This is because only a supernode subscribed to all column subnets can see rows being completed elsewhere and cancel duplicate work. Phase 3: after a delay longer than in phase 2 (TBD), any node that has joined a row subnet should recover rows that are still incomplete (SHOULD). It runs only when earlier phases fail, so the expected CPU cost is close to zero. All delays are measured from the moment the node first obtains a valid block root for that slot, and the duty attaches to only one block root per slot (the current head branch, or the first valid block root seen). Other block roots in the same slot are OPTIONAL, so double proposals cannot inflate the work. A row completed first through another path must cancel any pending reconstruction (MUST), and delays have a maximum value (TBD) so that recovery is not postponed indefinitely.

17m33kce0eh: The calldata of the verification operation is n * RECENT_ROOT_TUPLE_BYTES (72) bytes, with 1 <= n <= MAX_RECENT_ROOT_REFERENCES (16). Empty calldata, a length that is not a multiple of 72, and more than 16 tuples all revert, and none overlaps with the 64-byte write encoding. For each tuple it checks slot < current_slot, current_slot - slot <= RECENT_ROOT_USABLE_WINDOW (8191), and storage[storage_key] == entry_hash, and if any one fails the whole call reverts. Duplicate tuples are each checked separately, and if all pass, it succeeds with no return value, logs, or state changes. The current slot is read with SLOTNUM, no other account is called, and only storage keys derived from calldata are read. The recent root verifier frame that carries this operation has mode == VERIFY, target == RECENT_ROOT_ADDRESS, flags == 0, value == 0, limits.state == 0, and a data length that is a multiple of 72 between 72 and 16 * 72 inclusive. In public mempool classification it is called recent_root_verify. It executes with EIP-8141 STATICCALL semantics, and if the contract reverts or the frame halts exceptionally, the transaction becomes invalid. Gas is ordinary EVM gas, target access and storage reads follow the usual warm and cold rules, and data follows the EIP-8141 transaction data fee. By using a standard frame instead of an envelope field, EIP-8141's encoding, signature hash, execution, gas, and frame lookup are reused as they are, and the transaction payload and signature hash do not change either.

VERIFY_MLDSA44 is at 0x12, VERIFY_MLDSA65 at 0x13 and VERIFY_MLDSA87 at 0x14, corresponding to ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 in FIPS 204. The public key uses the FIPS 204 standard compressed encoding pk = (ρ, t1), and the signature uses the standard signature encoding. The sizes are fixed per parameter set. ML-DSA-44 has PK_LEN 1312 and SIG_LEN 2420, so the minimum input is 3732 bytes. ML-DSA-65 has 1952 and 3309, giving 5261 bytes. ML-DSA-87 has 2592 and 4627, giving 7219 bytes. There are three reasons for splitting addresses instead of using a single precompile that separates the three levels with a selector byte. Each address has a fixed input shape and gas, so no branch byte needs to be parsed. There is no room to confuse the selector with the first byte of the public key. And a chain can enable each level and set its gas price separately.

19lvc0k56x: On Ethereum, a log is an event record that a smart contract emits, and it can be written at a much lower gas cost than writing to state. However, the protocol does not provide an efficient way to look these logs up. The bloom filter in each block was reasonably useful early on, but it is now saturated and practically useless. As a result, most users depend on remote providers (RPC services), which cannot prove that their query results are correct. If a contract sits on a trustless distributed ledger but its output has to be taken on trust, the original purpose is defeated. As Ethereum's throughput grows, this information asymmetry gets worse. This EIP proposes an index structure that can be updated far more cheaply than the state trie while still allowing lookup results to be verified with moderately sized proofs. The goal is to increase the usefulness of logs while keeping their low gas cost.

1aetdhj6abu: After activation, ecRecover at address 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000001 behaves in the following order. (1) It consumes 3000 gas and aborts with out of gas if gas is insufficient. (2) It recovers the ECDSA public key from the input (hash, v, r, s) as it does today, and returns empty output if recovery fails. (3) If recovery succeeds, it computes the code check cost under EIP-8038. Whether the account is cold or warm is decided from accessed_addresses before the account is read. This is the pre-state gas check of EIP-7928. If recovered_address is not in accessed_addresses, the cost is COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS (3000). If it is, the cost is WARM_ACCESS (100). One more WARM_ACCESS (100) is added as the code lookup fee. This fee is not waived even if the code is empty or the account is rejected by the later check. (4) It consumes that cost and aborts with out of gas if gas is insufficient, in which case no account access occurs. 1cemwuzknn1: As in EIP-2200, the original value is the slot's value at the start of the transaction, and the current value is the value just before the SSTORE. The cost is the sum of three components. The access component is COLD_STORAGE_ACCESS if the slot is cold and WARM_ACCESS if it is warm. The write component STORAGE_WRITE is charged only when the new value differs from the current value and the current value equals the original value, that is, only when the slot is first moved away from its value at the start of the transaction. The state creation component GAS_STORAGE_SET is charged as state gas under EIP-8037 when the original and current values are 0 and the new value is nonzero. Refund rules are evaluated on every SSTORE. First, if the original and current values are nonzero and the new value is 0, STORAGE_CLEAR_REFUND is added. Second, if the original value is nonzero, the current value is 0 and the new value is nonzero, STORAGE_CLEAR_REFUND is subtracted. This reverses the first rule so that clearing and then refilling a slot in the same transaction does not yield a gain. Third, if the new value equals the original value and differs from the current value, STORAGE_WRITE is refunded. Without this reversal, a round trip from x to 0 and back to x would leave a net refund even though the slot is unchanged. Across the whole transaction, a slot that ends with a changed value pays the write and creation components exactly once, and a slot that ends at its original value pays only the access cost. Refunds accumulate in the transaction refund counter and are applied only up to 20% of total gas used. The refill rules for state gas are in EIP-8037.

1cq86w4x4c: Today, for a smart contract to send ether to another address, it must call that address. A call hands the execution flow to the other party, so even if you only want to send money, the recipient's code runs too. This causes several problems. Reentrancy attacks are possible, where the recipient calls the sender back. Denial of service attacks are also possible, where the recipient uses up all the gas or reverts execution to block the transfer itself. The 2300 gas that comes with every call by default cannot modify regular storage, but it can modify transient storage (EIP-1153), which leaves room for unintended state changes. Running code also costs gas, so you pay more even if you only want to send funds. Future call-family instructions may have no way to limit the amount of gas passed on. Also, since EIP-7702 lets a regular account (EOA) delegate to code, even a transfer to an ordinary wallet address now executes code and uses gas. A dedicated instruction that only sends ether avoids all of these problems at once.

If an ASSERT failure removed the transaction from the block and also reverted the gas payment, it would become a DoS path where an attacker spends up to the block gas limit and reverts for free, so the transaction is kept valid and the gas is still charged. No new gas constants were added. The slots and accounts in the difference were already written by the transaction and are therefore warm, and reading them with SLOAD or BALANCE costs WARM_STORAGE_READ_COST, so the same value is charged, and values such as counts or addresses were also priced uniformly. A client can build an index of the difference and logs once, when the ASSERT frame first reads, and reuse it, and that cost is covered by the access costs and LOG costs the transaction has already paid. The reason events are used as the transfer channel is that EIP-8141 discards transient storage between frames and does not provide the return data of earlier frames, so length-capable events are the only way to pass pre-execution values to the ASSERT frame. For state changes, a slot written many times through reentrant calls is still one entry, so execution order cannot give a deterministic order, and they are sorted by address and slot key, while events have a log index and use the order of occurrence.

1ey9vezsmk5: Setting the multiplier as the gap between the current slot's offline balance and a slowly moving average has three consequences. First, at the start of a simultaneous failure the multiplier jumps in proportion to the size of the outlier, and then falls over roughly a day as the moving average absorbs the event. Operators are penalized for being correlated and less so for recovering slowly. Second, the starting multiplier is 1 + PENALTY_SLOPE * spike, which gives about 9x for a 1% simultaneous failure, about 39x for 5%, about 78x for 10%, and about 154x for 20%. Because PENALTY_SLOPE = 3 * (MAX_PENALTY_FACTOR - 1), the cap is reached at exactly one third. Third, when participation is stable the multiplier is exactly 1 in every slot. The individual multiplier is kept linear. The affected stake and the multiplier are each linear, so the network-wide penalty is already quadratic in the size of the event, and a convex multiplier would push the total to cubic while removing the deterrent in the 1 to 15% range where operator choices matter. The draft's NET_EXCESS_PENALTIES counter was replaced with an explicit moving average because the cap barely affects the total penalty, because at mainnet participation rates its equilibrium sits below 1 and it oscillates near 0, and because at deterrent-scale events its recovery window stretches to several months.

After the Capella upgrade made conversion to 0x01 possible, the number of 0x00 validators fell from about 600,000 to about 9,200 as of August 2026. However, conversions have slowed to the low double digits per month, and several hundred have not attested for more than six months and appear to have lost their keys. 1g8b3yx8qzn: Ethereum does not yet have a post-quantum signature verifier that contracts can call. ML-DSA is a signature scheme based on lattice mathematics, and it is the first lattice signature that the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published as a final standard (FIPS 204). Cloud key management services and hardware security modules already generate ML-DSA keys at three security levels and sign with them, and certificate and transport protocol specifications use the same FIPS 204 encoding. A precompile that accepts that encoding as is can verify signatures made by any device, and a key owner can protect an account with that key without ever taking the key out. EIP-8051 has the same goal, but it covers only security level II (ML-DSA-44) and fixes the message to a 32-byte hash. This proposal judges that an account authentication key protects funds for years and therefore needs more margin than 128 bits. So it includes the higher security levels III and V as well, and leaves the message length free, exactly as in FIPS 204.
1g8cro802o1: An Ethereum node is split into an execution layer (EL) and a consensus layer (CL). The execution layer actually executes transactions and holds state such as account balances. Today, however, there is no protocol-level minimum for how long the execution layer must keep past state. Old block data is covered by the history expiry rules, but when to delete state is left to each client. A problem arises when a reorg occurs, in which the chain a node was following switches to a different branch. To validate the new branch, the node must re-execute from the state at the point where the two branches diverged. If that state has already been deleted, the node has to sync again from the beginning. The divergence point cannot be deeper than the last finalized block. The length of time finality can stall is capped by the consensus layer's inactivity leak. This proposal closes the gap by setting a single retention period matched to that cap.

1hu8wsq9u6t: The threat model assumes a permissionless environment where Sybil attacks are free. There are four main scenarios. A DoS that drains mempool resources with partially disclosed transactions can be detected by nodes that request the full payload. An attack that selectively withholds the transaction data of a specific L2 is mitigated by a large and diverse peer set. Eclipse attacks are mitigated by periodically rotating connections and tracking the full announcement rate of neighbors, and free riders by tracking the request-to-announcement ratio and blocking them. Custody-aligned sampling has a predictable request pattern, so a victim could be attacked by an adversary that stores only the few columns the victim will sample while impersonating a provider. To prevent this, the EIP introduces sampling noise: requests to a provider include at least one additional random column, and failure to serve that column is treated as a strong signal of misbehavior. The overhead per request is negligible at about 12KiB. Normative peer scoring that statistically tracks the request-to-announcement ratio was excluded from standardization because of its rigidity and left to each implementation's local heuristics.

1igu7tihhri: Today, verifying a beacon block requires re-executing the execution payload inside it against the full execution layer (EL) state. This needs all account and storage data, and the cost of re-execution grows in proportion to the gas limit. As a result, the hardware a node needs is tied to the chain's throughput and state size. As the gas limit rises or the state grows, the hardware threshold for becoming a validator rises with it. This EIP separates nodes that produce proofs from nodes that check proofs. It opens a path for the checking side to confirm payload validity in constant time without EL state. However, because proof systems are still maturing, the EIP does not make them mandatory from the start. Instead, only nodes that want to turn them on do so, building operating experience and metrics on a real network. There is no reward for proof-generating nodes, so participation is considered voluntary.

1itcgmc3akn: Register machines such as x86, ARM and RISC-V keep the return address in a link register or in a single stack mixed with data. Stack machines such as Forth, the JVM, Wasm and the CLR, by contrast, effectively use separate data and return stacks. The EVM is a stack machine, so it adopts the same proven approach. Another reason is that data stack items are 32 bytes while a jump destination needs only a byte or two. Because the return address lives only on its own stack and cannot be read, modified or moved with ordinary stack operations, the class of vulnerabilities in which code corrupts its own control flow disappears entirely. The remaining risks are checked at execution time as defined by the instructions.

1ivstilus5p: There are now many EVM chains, and most developers want to deploy a contract at the same address on every chain. When addresses differ between chains, apps and wallets have to maintain separate per-chain address lists, and because smart contract accounts get deployed at different addresses on different chains, there have been real cases of lost funds. The CREATE2 opcode supports deployments with predetermined addresses, but the created address is computed from the address of the contract that executes the opcode, so a factory that exists at the same address on every chain is needed first. Until now, this factory has been deployed with a keyless transaction that anyone can broadcast as is, but that transaction has a fixed gas price and limit, so deployment was often impossible on chains with different gas rules. Gas schedule changes have started to cause the same problem on Ethereum itself and on devnets, so the proposal aims to guarantee the existence of the already widely used factory through the rules themselves.

Even in the worst case, only TABLE_SIZES[len(TABLE_SIZES)-1] * 5 // 4 - 1 recent blocks, which is 319 blocks with the current parameters, are enough to build the top-level table root. In a fully stateless protocol, merging can be implemented using witnesses of partially merged tables. 1j4sa6by52v: The first byte of every key is the zone identifier Z. 0x00 is the account header, 0x01 is a code chunk, 0xFF is storage, and 0x02 to 0xFE are reserved for future categories. A key is assembled from the zone byte, a hash-determined tree position, and a 1-byte sub-index, and the zone byte and tree position together are called the stem. One stem has STEM_SUBTREE_WIDTH = 256 sub-indexes. Key lengths are fixed per zone: ACCOUNT_KEY_LENGTH and CODE_KEY_LENGTH are 34 bytes, and STORAGE_KEY_LENGTH is 66 bytes. Fixing a single length within a zone guarantees prefix-free, and keys in different zones differ from the first byte. Addresses are passed as Address32, the 20-byte address prefixed with 12 zero bytes.

A 10% cut in the blob fee can move the total cost by only 0.0000001%, so the fee keeps falling and ends up stuck at 1 wei, the smallest unit of ether. If demand returns in this state, nearly full blocks have to continue for over an hour before the price recovers its equilibrium. In the meantime users are pushed into first-come bidding competition and the experience gets worse. Swings in resource usage also get in the way of scaling blob space. In addition, nodes perform KZG proof verification, an expensive cryptographic check, for every blob, and at a 1 wei fee blob users barely pay for that computation.

1jd7irwhp5t: The FOCIL (EIP-7805) data structure is extended to [transactions, recursive_stark], so an inclusion list, like a block, carries the dependency proof for its own transactions. 1jnrcsmry6f: A quantum-safe hash-based signature is about 2 to 3 kB each and costs 150,000 to 200,000 gas to verify. Lattice-based signatures cost about the same. STARKs (Scalable Transparent ARguments of Knowledge), which are hash-based zero-knowledge proofs, exceed 128 kB and grow to 512 kB if they are to be generated quickly on a user's device, so verification needs millions of gas. Putting this data into a transaction as it is makes privacy protocols too expensive to use and makes it incompatible with FOCIL (EIP-7805), the inclusion list mechanism, and with frame transactions (EIP-8141). This EIP solves the problem by leaving only a light declaration in the transaction, having the mempool verify the actual signatures and proofs and merge them into one recursive STARK, so that a block carries only that single proof.

For that guarantee to hold, previously deployed old code, which was never validated, must not be mistaken for the new format by accident. 1jx4mmopvj6: Solidity has checked arithmetic overflow (a result exceeding the representable range) by default since version 0.8.0, and Vyper since the start. However, the EVM itself has no instruction that performs this check, so the compiler inserts a multi-instruction check for every operation. As a result, an addition that should cost 3 gas costs about 79 gas in Solidity, so safety costs 25 times as much. Because the cost is burdensome, developers are tempted to turn off checks with workarounds such as unchecked blocks or unsafe_add, and code that disables checks even where safety is not proven grows more common and harder to audit. There are real attacks that exploited unchecked subtraction. This proposal adds instructions with the check built in directly to the EVM, lowering the cost of a safe addition to 5 gas and removing the reason to bypass the check at all.
1jxdm5hzheu: The extra cost is computed as EXCESS_CODE_COST = ceil32(excess_code_size(len(code))) * GAS_PER_CODE_WORD // 32. Since excess_code_size(n) = max(0, n - 0x6000), code of 0x6000 (24576 bytes) or less has zero excess, and for larger code only the length beyond that is counted. ceil32 is a function that rounds up to a multiple of 32 bytes. GAS_PER_CODE_WORD is 2, so each word (32 bytes) of excess is charged 2 additional gas. Plugging into the formula, code of 65536 bytes, the maximum under EIP-7954, has 40960 bytes of excess, which is 1280 words, so 2560 gas is added. The accompanying constants COLD_SLOAD_COST 2100, WARM_STORAGE_READ_COST 100, and COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST 2600 are taken unchanged from EIP-2929. 1kc28qfik2i: Today a single transaction can in theory use the entire block gas limit by itself. Such very large transactions carry three risks. First, one transaction can monopolize the block processing load and become a channel for denial-of-service (DoS) attacks that shake the network. Second, transactions that use a lot of gas usually cause large state changes, which quickly inflates the data nodes must store. Third, block validation takes longer, which hurts user experience and network decentralization. These risks grow as the block gas limit rises. Capping the gas a single transaction can use reduces the single-transaction DoS risk, distributes gas more evenly within a block, and prevents extreme block validation times, which stabilizes synchronization between nodes.

1kh9wa4mhy6: The input is a single big-endian byte string with no header and no length fields. Starting at offset 0, the first PK_LEN bytes are the pubkey, the next SIG_LEN bytes are the signature, and the remaining len(input) - PK_LEN - SIG_LEN bytes are the message. With L = len(input), if L < PK_LEN + SIG_LEN, the precompile MUST return failure (32 zero bytes) without reverting. L == PK_LEN + SIG_LEN is a valid input with an empty message, because FIPS 204 allows an empty message. Putting the message last and dropping the length field is a choice to keep input assembly simple. You write the two fixed-length fields first, append the message, and call with that size, so there is no length word to compute or misplace. It also matches how the witness arrives. In EIP-8141, an ML-DSA witness can arrive as an ARBITRARY signature entry holding pubkey ++ signature, and a VERIFY frame moves it into memory with a single SIGPARAM copy. Appending the message that the signature approves after that makes it the precompile input without repackaging or rescanning the witness bytes.
1kj3cuhn394: CALL can in general cause any side effect, so static analyzers and optimizers have to treat it conservatively. Even if a special case is made for precompiles, a future hard fork could change the effect of CALL, so analysis results for code that uses the identity precompile are valid only for a particular block range. MCOPY, by contrast, is known at the instruction level to affect only memory. A dedicated instruction also means that memory copy costs are unaffected if the gas costs of the CALL family change in the future. The EIP text also cites as grounds that memory copying was found to be a large overhead in computation-heavy work such as EVM384.

1ku4z7qjsir: The entity that writes a root is identified by source_id = keccak256(source_address || salt). source_address can be an externally owned account or a contract, and varying the salt lets one address hold multiple sources. Who may write and how salts are allocated are the app's responsibility. The stored value is entry_hash = keccak256(RECENT_ROOT_ENTRY_DOMAIN || source_id || uint64_be(slot) || root), and the storage location is storage_key = keccak256(RECENT_ROOT_STORAGE_DOMAIN || source_id || uint64_be(i)), where i = slot mod RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH. Each source effectively has a ring buffer entries: bytes32[RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH] of length 8192, and every cell starts at 0. Slots and indexes are 8-byte big-endian, addresses are 20 bytes, and domains, roots, salts, source_ids, hashes, and keys are concatenated as fixed 32-byte lengths. Because the stored value is a hash that contains source_id, slot, and root together, a check cannot be passed with another source's root or with an old root left in the same cell. There is no separate source creation transaction. A source comes into existence on the first write with a new (source_address, salt), and a write that creates a new storage cell usually pays the state growth cost. Total storage grows in proportion to the number of source_ids written, and each source writes at most RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH keys.

The principle is a single one: accept only a message that carries at least one vote not seen before. A single attestation already seen, a second batch from the same batcher, and a batch whose members are all already known are silently dropped as IGNORE. As a result, an attacker holding k committee keys can get at most k messages per duty through, and since each message needs a valid attestation, seal, and batcher signature, the bandwidth the attacker consumes is proportional to the attacker's own signing cost. For SECP256K1 and P256, signer is a 20-byte address, and if it is empty it is taken to be tx.sender. For ARBITRARY, signer must be empty. If msg is empty, the signature is over compute_sig_hash(tx), and if it is 32 bytes, the signature is over that digest. A 32-byte value of all zeros is invalid. A SECP256K1 signature is 65 bytes of v || r || s, where v must be 0 or 1 and s must be low-s. P256 is 128 bytes of r || s || qx || qy, and signer must equal keccak256(qx || qy)[12:]. All signatures verified by the protocol must pass before frame execution, and if any one fails the transaction is invalid. The signature hash is computed as keccak(0x06 || rlp(tx)) after replacing the signature bytes of each signature with an empty msg by its length (an integer), so a signer must know the byte length of every empty-msg signature before signing. The raw bytes of protocol-verified signatures cannot be read from the EVM, to allow future aggregation, and only ARBITRARY signatures can be read with SIGDATACOPY.

1ok8nnk5pfl: An atomic batch is a contiguous range from frame i to frame j (j > i), where ATOMIC_BATCH_FLAG is set on frames i through j-1 and unset on j. If one frame in the batch fails, the state is reverted to just before the batch started and the remaining frames are skipped. The logs and state changes of frames that ran earlier are discarded, but the receipt keeps their execution status and execution gas used, empties the logs, and sets state gas to 0. The execution and state gas assigned to skipped frames is refunded at the end of the transaction. Inside a batch APPROVE is not possible, so there is never a need to roll back payer or sender_approved. The receipt payload is [cumulative_gas_used, payer, [frame_receipt, ...]], where frame_receipt is [status, gas_used, logs] and gas_used is [execution, state]. A new status code 0x2 is added to status, meaning a frame skipped because of a batch failure. The receipt has no transaction-level status, so an interface that must show a single status has to derive it itself. The logs bloom and log indices are the logs of the frame receipts concatenated in frame order. Between frames, TSTORE/TLOAD transient storage is discarded, and warm/cold records are shared across frames but are reverted along with a frame if that frame reverts.

1osknx6syw9: Ethereum nodes keep transactions that are not yet in a block in a waiting area called the mempool, and exchange them with each other. For small transactions, a node pushes the body directly to a few neighbors, but the remaining nodes, as well as large transactions and type 3 transactions that carry blobs, receive only an announcement that "this transaction exists." Today this announcement contains only the hash, type, and size. The receiving node has nothing to judge by except the order in which announcements arrived, so when it spreads requests across several neighbors, it easily ends up fetching transactions that cannot be included in a block because of gaps in the nonce (the per-account sequence number) of the same account. Even when it tries to fill a gap, it does not know whose transaction with which number is missing, so the only option is to request one more hash at a time. To filter out stale announcements for transactions already on chain, it has to keep the hashes of every transaction on chain in a cache. There is also no way to request only the transactions of a particular sender. As block throughput grows, nodes will increasingly be unable to fetch every transaction, so they need information that lets them pick what to fetch and fill gaps.

1pxrznh5nks: This EIP changes DAS networking but leaves PeerDAS custody assignment and its probabilistic guarantees untouched. Row distribution is an additional recovery path and the existing paths stay almost unchanged, so the added cost is limited to the bitmap signaling and, when data is partially withheld, wasted cell requests of at most half a row per assigned row for each row subnet member. Every reconstruction obligation is conditioned on holding 64 verified cells, so unavailable data cannot be used to trigger reconstruction CPU work. The one exception is that phase 2 full reconstruction is deliberately delayed, which implementations already do in practice, and the delay is a single one rather than a delay at every hop. An attack in which a block producer withholds a single cell from one row and releases 64 columns' worth of cells for the remaining rows, causing recovery work on a block that will end up unavailable, is inherited from PeerDAS. In PeerDAS every supernode duplicates this work, but here phase 1 divides it to about one row per row reconstructor and phase 2 skips completed rows, so total work goes down. A supernode sees the bitmaps of all columns, so it can notice unrecoverable rows and skip the work for that block. Row distribution is only an optimization, so a node MUST NOT change its sampling or availability decision rules, or delay a decision, based on row subnet state, and the column topics and request/response remain the authoritative path. Sending a bitmap per cell can make message complexity grow quadratically, so debouncing, rate limiting, and a cap on the number of GroupIDs tracked per peer are recommended. A peer that does not repeatedly deliver cells it has advertised is handled in peer scoring like a peer that sends late messages. Row subnet assignment is a public function of the node ID, so an attacker could grind node IDs to take over or isolate a particular subnet, but phase 2 reconstruction and the column topics cover that row, so the impact is limited to falling back to the current state.

1ql0ayrc1my: process_randao takes the hash-chain path if the stored commitment is not 0. It checks that hash_chain_reveal is not 0, that blake3(HASH_CHAIN_RANDAO_DST + reveal) equals the stored commitment, and that randao_reveal is G2_POINT_AT_INFINITY. It then accumulates mix = blake3(existing mix + reveal) and stores the revealed value as the new commitment. If the commitment is 0, it verifies the BLS signature as before and mixes with xor. The hash-chain path uses a hash accumulator instead of xor because of the commitment-copying attack. A commitment carries no identity, so someone can copy another validator's current commitment to create a valid registration, and with a linear xor accumulator they could cancel the victim's contribution by inserting the same value again. A hash has no efficient inverse operation, so inserting the same value again just yields an unrelated new mix, and this attack is blocked at the root. That is why the raw reveal value can be mixed in without per-validator personalization. The assertion that rejects a 0 reveal protects the invariant that 0 means unregistered.

1qn7uzm6830: A BAL is an RLP list that follows the order address → field → block access index → change. For each account it records AccountChanges = [address, storage_changes, storage_reads, balance_changes, nonce_changes, code_changes]. BlockAccessIndex is 0 for pre-execution system calls, 1..n for transactions in block order, and n+1 for post-execution, including withdrawals. Integer fields (StorageKey, StorageValue, Balance, Nonce, BlockAccessIndex) must be encoded as minimal big-endian with no leading zeros, and 0 is encoded as an empty byte string (0x80). Because the hash commits to these bytes, using a different encoding for the same value, such as 32-byte padding, makes the block invalid. Ordering is also enforced. Accounts are sorted lexicographically by address, slots and read keys by key ascending, and each change list by index ascending. Each address must appear exactly once in the list, and the same slot cannot appear in both storage_changes and storage_reads.

1rwzftkvnuv: The existing delegation indicator in EIP-7702 is 0xef0100 || delegate_address, and the 0xef0101 || delegate_address added by this EIP is an ECDSA-disabled delegation. ECDSA-disabled means the original ECDSA key can no longer authorize transactions or EIP-7702 delegation changes. It does not mean the delegation target is frozen forever. Wallet code can update the delegation target while keeping the ECDSA-disabled state. There is one irreversible invariant: once ECDSA authority is turned off, it is never restored. 1rwzyk4f0rz: The host (usually a stateful EL client) records the account, storage, code, and ancestor header data it uses while executing or building a block. build_stateless_input bundles the ExecutionWitness, ExecutionRequests, the block access list, and chain_id into a StatelessInput. The execution witness is built from the per-block read/write tracker that the EL already uses to build the block access list (BAL), together with pre-state trie data. The host records trie nodes using the same lookups the guest uses when reading, and both sides apply inserts and updates first and deletions afterward in each storage trie. A deletion can collapse a branch, and then the remaining sibling node is needed. Doing deletions last reduces collapses, and because both sides write in the same order, the guest never looks for a sibling node the host did not record. build_execution_witness finally asserts that mpt_root equals the expected post-state root. On serialization, a 2-byte schema ID is prepended to the SSZ bytes. The high byte is the fork (Amsterdam = 0x15) and the low byte is the schema revision, so Amsterdam revision 1 is 0x1501. The guest must accept only the canonical SSZ encoding, and the reference decoder re-encodes the decoded value and rejects the input if the bytes are not exactly the same. This check catches offset gaps and unread trailing bytes, even inside nested containers. Conformance tests must be run with the blockchain_test_engine fixture, not blockchain_test. Because StatelessInput wraps the Engine API NewPayloadRequest, the engine fixture covers more invalid payload variants.

1s5wi7s26j4: Row subnets carry only partial messages and do not define a full message form. A node that does not support the Partial Messages Extension must not subscribe to a row subnet (MUST NOT), and mesh peers that do not support the extension may be pruned (MAY). The non-discrimination guidance in EIP-8136 applies to column topics, which have a full-message fallback path, and for nodes without support the column topics and getBlobs remain open as before. Row subnet membership is computed from the node ID alone, so no ENR extension is needed. A node applies get_row_subnet to node IDs it finds through discv5 lookups and similar means to locate peers on the same subnet, and it should secure enough connections to maintain a healthy mesh (SHOULD). This is because subnet members make up only about 1 / ROW_SUBNET_COUNT of all nodes, so they do not appear often enough among random peers. The SSZ containers, bitmap encoding and GroupID derivation are defined in ethereum/consensus-specs following the EIP-8136 approach. The bitmap covers the rows assigned to the subnet in blob_index order, and within a row in cell_index order. Cells received from a row subnet must be verified against the KZG commitment of the corresponding blob before they are forwarded or used (MUST), and a peer that sends an invalid cell is penalized under the same rules as on column subnets. A peer may limit itself to providing only half of the cells of each assigned row (MAY), and this limit applies per row. 1t5ng7w7iv5: Today every transaction pays the same 21,000 base gas regardless of what it does. A zero-value transaction to an existing account and a transaction that creates a new account while sending funds pay the same amount. This is so even though the latter touches one more account, writes a new balance, emits a log, and increases the state that the blockchain must keep permanently. A single fixed constant is priced high for the simplest path and low for the path that uses genuinely long-lived resources. This proposal splits that constant into named items such as signature verification, account access, balance write, and new account creation, so that each transaction pays for what it actually does. Pricing the costs in the same units used elsewhere in the gas system also has the advantage that when the price of an individual item changes later, the change is reflected automatically without recalculating a separate constant.

1u58ajfv7dw: Signature permanence: The preregistration signature is fork-independent and never expires cryptographically. Only the onchain record has a window of 262,144 slots (about 36 days at 12-second slots), and anyone holding the signed message can resubmit it after expiry to revive the record. Operators must confirm that the credential they choose is supported in the intended withdrawal flow. Builder deposits: Preregistration applies only to validator deposits, and EIP-8282 builder deposits neither check nor consume it. Preregistering a 0xB0 credential does not register or protect a builder, and sending 0xB0 through the validator deposit path creates a validator that currently cannot withdraw. Race condition: If an attacker deposits before the registration is processed, first-deposit-wins creates the validator and the registration is rejected. If both are in the same payload, the deposit is processed first and the result is the same. So a protocol must verify the registration's existence and expiry atomically with the deposit via EIP-4788, and if it verifies in a separate transaction it must wait until inclusion is finalized. State size: Active records total at most about 46 MB (88 bytes × 524,288), plus up to MAX_PREREGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_PAYLOAD × (SLOTS_PER_EPOCH - 1) = 124 expired records waiting for the next cleanup. At the target rate of 1 per block, filling 2**19 takes about 72.8 days, which exceeds the 36-day expiry window, so in steady state the active count stays near 2**18 (about 23 MB), and saturating it requires a rate above target, which makes the fee rise exponentially. If n requests per block (n > 1) are sustained, excess grows by n - 1 per block, and the fee exceeds 1 ETH after about 17 × ln(10^18) / (n - 1) blocks.

The loss that liquidity providers on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) suffer to arbitrage is proportional to the square root of the block interval, so cutting 12 seconds to 10 seconds reduces it by about 9%. Shorter slots also bring final confirmation sooner, and more block proposers take part in the same span of time, which makes censoring transactions harder. The real bottleneck, though, is not choosing the number. The assumption that a slot is 12 seconds is embedded throughout every consensus client and execution client. This EIP does two things together: it first removes that assumption so that slot time becomes a configuration value, and then it conservatively reduces it to 10 seconds.

As block gas limits have grown, a single mainnet block now holds more than 1000 log addresses and topics on average, and the rate at which the filter wrongly answers that something is present (the false positive rate) has soared, making it practically useless. Restoring it to a usable level would require growing the filter about 10 times, which would enlarge the header to about 3 kilobytes, and even then finding a year of recent logs would require downloading more than 6 gigabytes of header data. Checking which block a transaction was included in also requires the bodies of every block in the search range. Full nodes and RPC servers build and use their own indexes, but these indexes cannot be verified remotely, so users end up having to trust the server. The starting point of this proposal is that no matter how much transaction throughput is increased, it goes against the purpose of Ethereum if there is no way to verify the results without trust.

1xxxcflbup0: The validation rules for the execution_proof topic follow the same [IGNORE]/[REJECT] convention as other beacon gossip topics. There are three IGNORE conditions. If the node has not yet seen the new_payload_request_root, it ignores the message, though it may queue it until the payload arrives. If a valid proof already exists for the (new_payload_request_root, proof_type) combination, it ignores the message, so only the first valid proof of each type is forwarded. If the (new_payload_request_root, proof_type, validator_index) combination is not the first, it ignores the message, giving each prover only one chance. REJECT applies when validator_index is not an active validator, when the BLS signature is wrong, when proof_data is empty or exceeds MAX_PROOF_SIZE, or when the process_execution_proof check fails, and the sender is penalized through the existing peer score. There are three req/resp messages. ExecutionProofsByRange takes (start_slot, count, proof_types) and is used for range backfill. ExecutionProofsByRoot takes a list of (block_root, List[proof_type]) identifiers and is used to look up proofs for specific blocks. ExecutionProofStatus sends and receives (block_root, slot, proof_types) to exchange the proof verification view and supported proof types, and the side that connects first must send it first. A client must answer both requests for canonical blocks within proof_serve_range, that is, [finalized_checkpoint.slot, current_slot], and if it cannot, it replies with 3: ResourceUnavailable and may be penalized. Discovery adds a uint8 ENR key, eproof, and a peer is treated as proof-aware if the value is present and nonzero. This works like the cgc field in Fulu, so advertising can be turned on and off without a fork or a fork version change.

1y8dfsfv555: The index space has one filter map for every interval of VALUES_PER_MAP (2**16) length. A filter map is a sparse bitmap of size MAP_WIDTH (2**24) x MAP_HEIGHT (2**16), and one bit is set per map value. Because each map holds a fixed number of values, VALUES_PER_MAP, the false positive probability stays constant. Maps are grouped into index epochs of MAPS_PER_EPOCH (2**10) maps each, and within an epoch the rows with the same row number are placed close together in the hash tree, so they can be fetched cheaply with a single Merkle multiproof. The native variant computes the payload blob commitments directly with blob_to_kzg_commitment and verifies payload_blob_count and the versioned hashes. It suits implementations before proofs become mandatory. The zkEVM-optimized variant takes into account that the multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) needed to compute commitments is expensive to prove inside a zkEVM circuit, so it batch-verifies polynomial opening proofs with verify_blob_kzg_proof_batch instead. 1z5z2rk26jm: A node can turn on proof-generation mode, proof-checking mode, or both. In generation mode, an active validator acts as a prover, produces execution proofs and publishes them on the execution_proof gossip topic. In checking mode, the node receives the propagated proofs and uses them as a supplementary signal for the validity of the corresponding payload. In this EIP phase, checking nodes also keep re-executing payloads, and verified proofs do not replace re-execution. The design keeps fork choice independent of proofs so that the proof stack can be measured under real network conditions. Proof generation and checking use the execution verification window introduced by EIP-7732. Because execution verification is deferred until the next beacon block, there is more time to produce proofs. There is no reward for proof-generating nodes, so the role is considered altruistic. In addition, independent of the request, generation and checking flow, proof-aware nodes must store proofs for canonical chain blocks up to the latest finalized checkpoint so that syncing peers can backfill. The source says only that a follow-up EIP may propose making proofs mandatory and removing re-execution.

1zaomap8k5k: If the burn were proportional to the rewards actually received, the marginal reward of every duty would shrink by a factor of (1 - b), weakening the incentive to participate correctly. So the burn is based on the reward the validator would have earned by performing perfectly, and it is deducted regardless of whether the validator actually performed. It does, however, reflect network-wide participation. The reward of a flawless attester also shrinks with network participation, and if the burn alone were charged on a full-participation basis, diligent validators would lose out whenever the offline share exceeds 1 - b. During an inactivity leak, when attestation rewards stop entirely, the attestation burn is paused in full. The reason for splitting by duty is the same. Taking one uniform deduction every epoch would keep the spec simple, but it would have to be large enough to cover the rarely occurring proposal and sync committee rewards, and as b grows it would exceed the attestation reward of an ordinary epoch. A validator that attests perfectly would then see its balance fall every epoch while waiting for its proposal turn. Charging per duty means a validator that attests diligently never goes negative merely because it has no proposal or sync committee assignment. The source explains that every base amount is determined only by network-wide aggregates, so no burn depends on the behavior of the validator that pays it, and a diligent validator keeps (1 - b) times the reward it received as net reward at any participation level.

1zi19sedc01: At the start of processing, the client checks tx.nonce == state[tx.sender].nonce, verifies all signatures, and then sets payer = None and sender_approved = false. Each frame starts on entry with gas_left = limits.execution and state_gas_left = limits.state, and first subtracts the warm/cold access cost (EIP-2929) of resolved_target. If the target has no code, the default code runs, and if it has an EIP-7702 delegation designator, the delegated code runs. APPROVE takes offset, length, and scope from the stack, ends the current call frame successfully, and changes the approval context. scope is one of APPROVE_PAYMENT (0x1), APPROVE_EXECUTION (0x2), or APPROVE_EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT (0x3), and must be within the range that frame.flags allows. If ADDRESS != resolved_target, it reverts. APPROVE_EXECUTION sets sender_approved to true only when resolved_target is tx.sender. APPROVE_PAYMENT, when sender_approved is true, payer is not yet set, and the balance is sufficient, increments the sender's nonce, sets payer = resolved_target, and collects max_cost. At this point, if the tx.sender account does not exist, STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT * CPSB of state gas is subtracted. Executing APPROVE outside a frame transaction halts with an exception. The frames up to the one where payer is set are the validation prefix, and the frames after that are the execution body. If payer is not set after all frames finish, the transaction is invalid.

1zity1tdxl: The biggest risk is false reassurance. An assertion with a narrow scope of checking leads people to believe a dangerous transaction is safe, so an incomplete assertion should be treated as the same as having none. The protocol does not force the inclusion of an ASSERT frame. A smart account must check in the VERIFY frame that its own ASSERT frame is present, and since ASSERT frames are gathered at the end, it can scan from the back. The target of an assertion must be an immutable contract that cannot be upgraded. Because the execution body runs before the assertion, the state the body can write can be chosen by an attacker. If the result of a call to an oracle, balanceOf, a registry or a proxy, or an after value, is used as the reference value, it can be manipulated, and a called contract can even run TXTRACE, notice that it is inside an ASSERT, and answer differently. The reference value must come from the data of an ASSERT frame fixed at signing time, or from a before value. An assertion constrains only that one transaction. An existing allowance or an off-chain permit is used in other transactions, and a pending withdrawal or a bridge deposit completes elsewhere. Changes by the verification prefix are visible but cannot be reverted, and events show only the fact that code emitted them, so storage and balances are the source of truth. Gas exhaustion is also a problem. Under the current settings a single transaction can emit about 42,600 events, and a malicious dapp can inflate the cost with cheap logs. An assertion must read the count first and check the limit, a framework must pass gas proportional to the expected count, and an assertion's OOG must always be treated as a revert. Sorted tables allow binary search, but events must be scanned in full. The verification prefix is not reverted, so untrusted execution must not be placed there, and a deploy frame must not be used for anything other than installing tx.sender code.

1zyaf3g8r1q: Today on Ethereum, deploying multiple contracts with the same code means paying to store the identical code again on every deployment. For cases that stamp out the same code repeatedly, such as token issuers, this cost simply accumulates. Proposals like EIP-8037, which reprices contract deployment in line with state growth, would make the burden even larger. Control over regular accounts (EOAs) is also a problem. Today an EOA can only initiate transactions with an ECDSA signature, and even when code is delegated through EIP-7702, only a delegation indicator is attached, so transactions signed with the original key remain valid. To protect an account by other means, such as a post-quantum (PQ) wallet, there must be a way to cut off ECDSA transaction authority, and there is no such way today. SETCODEFROM solves both problems with a single instruction. It first writes the per-account storage values, then adopts an already deployed shared code as its own code.

208e7k37ca9: To keep the validator set from centralizing, Ethereum has handed the right to build blocks to specialized firms called builders through an auction. As a result, a small number of sophisticated builders came to dominate block production, and the network's censorship resistance, its ability to stop specific transactions from being left out, got worse. Research followed on letting validators place constraints on builders, and the method is the inclusion list (IL), which forces transactions into a block. However, earlier inclusion list designs and proposals for joint block construction had problems with bribery and coercion attacks, list equivocation, account abstraction, and transaction invalidation. 21yj3gu21bv: Logs on Ethereum are a feature that lets apps record what happened on chain so they can find it easily later. A bloom filter is a summary structure that helps with that search. Its original goal was to quickly narrow down which blocks are relevant to your app without scanning the full history. In practice, however, this approach is far too slow. Most apps that query historical logs do not ask an Ethereum node directly and instead use centralized services outside the protocol. Even so, every client has to compute a bloom filter that no one uses each time it builds and validates a block. This proposal acknowledges that reality and proposes removing bloom filters from the protocol. Apps that need history queries are encouraged to use decentralized protocols that build verifiable log indexes with techniques such as zero-knowledge proofs.

Fork choice enforcement: forced inclusion is placed in the fork choice rule, the core of the consensus process, so no one can bypass it. A block that fails the conditions gets no attester votes, so it cannot become part of the canonical chain. Same slot: the list runs in parallel with building the slot N+1 block during slot N, so a transaction submitted in slot N can be enforced right away. This is a clear improvement over forward-looking list designs such as EIP-7547, which had a one-slot delay. Conditional inclusion: if a transaction cannot be appended to the end of the block or the block is full, some list transactions are accepted as missing. Position independence: it does not matter where in the block the list transactions appear, which reduces the incentive to route around the protocol through side channels, and combined with conditional inclusion, it makes an off-protocol market less attractive. The complexity of adding a fee scheme is judged not to be justified, and because the assumption is that only 1 of N committee members needs to be honest, the design relies on altruistic participation.

24e8xwzq5dx: Many EVM instructions take offset values as input, and these are often 0. For example, the return data parameters of the CALL family of instructions are set to 0 by contracts that use the RETURNDATA family of instructions. Currently, pushing 0 onto the stack requires PUSH1 0, which costs 3 gas at execution and takes 2 bytes of code, so deployment also costs 2 * 200 gas. To save this cost, it is common to use other instructions such as PC, MSIZE, CALLDATASIZE, RETURNDATASIZE, CODESIZE, CALLVALUE and SELFBALANCE as a stand-in for 0, which is risky because these values can vary with context. A mainnet analysis found that about 11.5% of executed PUSH-family instructions pushed 0, and across all existing accounts 340,557,331 bytes were spent on PUSH1 00, costing 68,111,466,200 gas to deploy. Creating a dedicated zero instruction makes code shorter and reduces such workarounds.

However, the original argues that this incentive never worked in practice, and that the state growth problem is now handled not by a cleanup reward but by pricing state directly when it is created (EIP-8037). Meanwhile, the burden refunds place on the protocol remains. The refund counter must be capped at 20% of gas used (EIP-3529), and this cap becomes intricately entangled with the calldata floor gas (EIP-7623/7976) and the two-dimensional gas accounting of EIP-8037. SELFDESTRUCT refunds, EIP-7702 per-authorization refunds, and block-level accounting of refunds have already been removed by earlier EIPs. Only the SSTORE refund rules remain. The part that refunds writes reverted within the same transaction is legitimate net charging, while the clearing refund is a cross-transaction incentive that no longer has a justification. This EIP removes only the latter.

26kx6cqom9k: Today every call that sends ether (CALL) carries an effective fixed charge of 9000 gas. The basis for this charge is the cost of writing account state at the end of the block, but that write happens only once per account whose balance changed, not once per transfer. So when ether moves back and forth between the same accounts several times within one transaction, the transaction repeatedly pays for state writes that will not actually happen. Contract storage has had net metering since EIP-2200, where changing a value is expensive only the first time and restoring the original value earns a refund, yet ether balances have no such rule. Ether is thus the only asset for which each repeated movement is billed like an independent state write. This cost works against common composition patterns such as relay and router contracts that pass received ether straight on, refund patterns that return the excess, and batch transfers that split funds among many recipients.

26tzyr5o60m: The cost of the identity precompile is 15 + 3 * (length / 32) gas plus call overhead. When the CALL cost rose to 700 it became effectively useless, and EIP-2929 lowered it to 100, but the EIP text still judges it too expensive to be a reasonable alternative. The MLOAD/MSTORE approach is fairly efficient at a minimum of 12 gas per word when offsets are known in advance and the loop can be unrolled, but copying with arbitrary offsets at execution time adds at least 6 more gas per word for the 32 ADD that advances the offset. There is a special case where, if the last piece is a single byte, it can be stored efficiently with MSTORE8, but handling partial words is costly overall. The floor only takes effect when execution is too cheap to cover it, and that is exactly the workaround situation. Adding X per SLOAD to intrinsic gas does not bound a block by gas_limit / 64. The optimal workaround still yields B = gas_limit / 64 + 24 · gas_limit / (2100 + X) bytes, and the residual term vanishes only when X becomes very large. A floor-side charge gives a closed upper bound directly. If every BAL byte is priced at FLOOR_GAS_PER_BYTE, the same as nonzero calldata, then whichever of calldata, delegation signatures, storage keys, addresses, code or balances the attacker picks, the floor gives 1/64 byte per gas, so the attacker's choice does not matter and the optimum converges to B = gas_limit / 64. Runtime extensions can make the floor bind even when execution gas does not, so they are checked against the execution gas budget. The first touch of an account warmed by EIP-2930 is a floor of 1,280 versus execution of 100, a warmed SLOAD is 2,048 versus 100, and a SELFDESTRUCT to a warmed but unmetered beneficiary is 84 × 64 = 5,376 versus 5,000. Deployed code is 64 per byte versus 200, and under EIP-8037 the code deposit execution charge is 6 gas per word, under 0.2 gas per byte, which makes it the trigger with the widest margin over the floor. Even so, the main bulk case is the calldata + SLOAD workaround, where the fixed seed of EIP-8131 is already close to the execution budget.

280zdbjyz7t: The prover runs the guest on the private input StatelessInput and produces the public output StatelessValidationResult. StatelessInput consists of new_payload_request, witness, and chain_id (uint64), and uses progressive containers and lists. The fixed bounds are MAX_EXTRA_DATA_BYTES = 32, MAX_WITNESS_HEADERS = 256, MAX_BYTES_PER_CODE = 2**16, MAX_BYTES_PER_HEADER = 2**10, and MAX_BYTES_PER_WITNESS_NODE = 2**10. In ExecutionWitness, state holds the raw RLP-encoded account and storage trie nodes needed for execution and state root recomputation, codes holds the bytecode read from the pre-state (excluding code deployed in the same block), and headers holds the RLP-encoded ancestor headers in block number order, ending at the payload's parent. The parent header is always included, and older headers go back as far as the oldest block returned by BLOCKHASH. The guest checks that the headers form a contiguous chain and uses their hashes to serve BLOCKHASH. The entry point run_stateless_guest decodes the SSZ input with its schema prefix, runs verify_stateless_new_payload, and serializes the result in every case. If decoding itself fails, it outputs a failure result in which the request root, chain_id, and schema_id are all zero, so a schema_id of 0 indicates that case. If validation fails after decoding, the decoded values are kept. WitnessState replaces the local pre-state DB by serving account, storage, and code reads from the witness, and it computes the post-state root from the block diff. The absence of a key is accepted only when the witness contains a trie path that proves the absence, and if a node on the path or a bytecode is missing or corrupted, the whole validation fails. The Amsterdam guest in the reference implementation does not compare the timestamp with fork activation, but production implementations must do so.

284parl0ool: An Ethereum block header contains the state root, a summary value of the ledger after executing all of that block's transactions. Computing this value is a major bottleneck in block production. During the MEV auction, where builders compete over which combination of transactions is most profitable, a builder must recompute the state root every time it changes the combination, so it ends up computing it thousands of times per slot. Once ePBS (EIP-7732) is introduced, builders will have even less time to spare. Block-Level Access Lists (BAL, EIP-7928), the list of storage locations a block touched, parallelize state reads and writes, but the state root is only known once execution finishes, so they do not help within the same slot. This proposal places the state root in the header one block later, so validators can attest to a block's validity without waiting for the state root computation.

Developers today want to bundle several calls and send them together. Many smart accounts can execute them atomically (all succeed or all are cancelled) within a single transaction. Validators must not delay block validation or attestation production while waiting for a proof, and if a proof is missing or late they follow the fork choice determined by the execution engine's re-execution. An asymmetry between checkers and provers is also pointed out. 2b9btjfyof7: For GasToken to stop working, no more gas must be extractable from a slot than was put into it. The source derives the condition by pairing each refund with an earlier expenditure on the same slot in the same transaction. If the event that clears a slot whose original value is nonzero to zero is the first one in that transaction, it can be paired with the minimum cost of first reading and modifying that slot, SSTORE_RESET_GAS + ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST. If it is the second or later, the earlier write that moved the value away from zero deducted SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE from the refund counter, so the two cancel out. Therefore, if SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE <= SSTORE_RESET_GAS + ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST, total gas expenditure per slot is always positive, and this EIP lowers SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE to exactly that sum. Intuitively, the design leaves no net refund when clearing data that has not yet been read (usually useless), and leaves a net refund when clearing data that has been read (more likely to be useful).

2bdk3f85ypq: Pure reads such as SLOAD, BALANCE, EXTCODESIZE, EXTCODECOPY, EXTCODEHASH, and call instructions that do not change state MUST NOT update last_written_block. There are three reasons. If reads changed the field, every old read would lead to a trie leaf rewrite and a state root recomputation, attaching write-level cost to reads. Also, data in the stable tier would be moved to the mutable tier by reads alone, creating write amplification and contradicting the goal of separating the mutable path. Finally, this field is consensus state reflected in the state root, so if reads changed it, EIP-214's guarantee that state does not change during STATICCALL would be broken. When a call frame reverts, the field is restored to its pre-frame value exactly like balance, nonce, and storage, and updates attached to rolled-back state changes MUST NOT be left behind.

2bhvlbc7de8: The gas limit increase that EIP-7732 makes possible means larger execution payloads. Larger payloads take longer to spread across the network. If a Payload Timeliness Committee (PTC) member does not receive the payload within the attestation deadline, even a valid payload is treated as missing. With the current execution_payload gossip topic, two problems become more pronounced as payloads grow. First, a node that has already received a large message has difficulty cutting off duplicate transmissions arriving by other paths midway, so the same bytes arrive multiple times and consume bandwidth that could carry new data. Second, a node can pass a message on only after receiving all of it, so each hop (one step of forwarding between nodes) adds one full transmission and the delay grows in proportion to message size times hop count. Splitting the message into chunks reduces both problems. At the chunk level no large duplicates can occur, and a node can forward a chunk as soon as it receives it, so hops proceed overlapped instead of queuing one after another.

2bxgg0x3d3f: The current CALL_VALUE under EIP-8038 is ACCOUNT_WRITE + CALL_STIPEND = 11300, and if the unused stipend of 2300 is returned the effective cost is 9000.
